overview.title: Logits, training results, and greedy decoding
overview.main_topic: A sidebar defining logits and from_logits=True, the result of pretraining (about 36% next-token accuracy, undertrained), and the start of 16.2.3 with Listing 16.9, a simple greedy autoregressive generation loop
overview.central_idea: Mini-GPT outputs logits (unnormalized log probabilities); softmax turns them into probabilities, and Keras lets you put that softmax in the loss instead of the model. After one pass over the data the model guesses the next token about 36% of the time and is clearly undertrained. Text is generated by repeatedly feeding the sequence in, taking the most likely next token at the last position, appending it and repeating.
overview.importance: Logits are the raw material for every sampling strategy that follows (p.505-508), and Listing 16.9 is the baseline generation loop that the next pages speed up (p.503) and improve (p.505).
learning_objectives: Define a logit and relate logits to probabilities through softmax
Explain the two ways to place the softmax in a Keras classifier and when from_logits=True is needed
Interpret the 36% next-token accuracy and why the model is undertrained
Describe autoregressive greedy decoding and trace Listing 16.9 line by line
Explain why argmax over logits equals argmax over probabilities

summary:
A sidebar, **"What is a logit?"**, explains the new loss argument seen in Listing 16.8 (p.501), `SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True)`. The output projection at the end of mini-GPT has **no softmax**; its outputs can be thought of as **unnormalized log probabilities**, one per vocabulary token. Exponentiating them and normalizing them to sum to 1, which is all `softmax` does, yields probabilities. An unnormalized log probability is called a **logit**, and logits are easier to work with when generating text (as the next section shows). Keras lets you choose where the softmax lives: either as the model's last activation (model outputs probabilities) or inside the loss (model outputs logits, and you pass `from_logits=True`).

Back in the main text, the trained model predicts the next token correctly **about 36% of the time** on the validation set, which the authors call a crude heuristic. The model is **undertrained**: validation loss keeps decreasing every epoch, unsurprising with 100x fewer training steps than GPT-1; more training would help but costs time and money.

Section **16.2.3 Generative decoding** reuses the approach of chapter 15 (Shakespeare and Spanish translation): feed a prompt, read the model's distribution over the vocabulary for the next token at every position, **select the most likely token at the last position, append it and repeat**, producing a sequence one token at a time. **Listing 16.9** implements this as `generate(prompt, max_length=64)`: tokenize the prompt into a Python list, then for `max_length - prompt_length` iterations call `mini_gpt` on the whole current sequence, take the logits at position `[0, -1]`, append `np.argmax(...)` as an int, and finally detokenize all tokens, prompt included.

paragraphs.excerpt: As we compile our model, you will notice a new value for the loss
paragraphs.what_it_says: The sidebar starts by pointing out the new loss setting used when compiling mini-GPT, SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True), and asks what a logit is.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Earlier classifiers in the book typically ended with a softmax and used the default from_logits=False. Listing 16.8 (p.501) breaks that habit, so the authors pause to explain it.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Mismatching the model's output and the loss's from_logits setting is a silent bug: training runs, but on the wrong objective.

terminology.meaning: Loss-function flag stating whether predictions are raw scores (True) or probabilities (False, the default).

connections: p.501: Listing 16.8 compiles mini-GPT with this loss

paragraphs.excerpt: The output projection at the end of our transformer model does not contain
paragraphs.what_it_says: Mini-GPT's output projection has no softmax. Its outputs are 'unnormalized log probabilities' for each token; exponentiating and normalizing them to sum to 1 (all softmax does) gives probabilities. Such a value is called a logit, and logits can be easier to work with when generating text.
paragraphs.what_it_means: If p_i = softmax(z)_i, then z_i = log p_i + C for some constant C shared by all tokens. That constant (the log of the normalizer) is why logits are 'unnormalized': they carry the same information as log probabilities up to a shift. Practical consequences: the argmax of the logits is the argmax of the probabilities, dividing logits by a temperature reshapes the distribution (p.506), and samplers such as keras.random.categorical accept logits directly (p.505).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Working in logit space is numerically safer (no log of tiny probabilities) and makes sampling tricks simple arithmetic on the logits, which the next pages exploit.
paragraphs.technical_idea: softmax is invariant to adding a constant to all logits: softmax(z + c) = softmax(z).

terminology.meaning: An unnormalized log probability: a real-valued score whose softmax gives a probability.
exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j); turns a vector of scores into a probability distribution.
The final mapping from hidden size 512 to vocabulary size 32,000; in mini-GPT it is the reverse embedding.

connections: p.500: outputs = embedding(x, reverse=True) is the output projection
p.505: keras.random.categorical applies softmax to logits and samples
p.506: temperature divides the logits before softmax

paragraphs.excerpt: Keras gives you a choice of where to apply the `softmax` function
paragraphs.what_it_says: For classification you can use softmax as the model's final activation and output probabilities, or move the softmax into the loss and output logits; for the latter, pass SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True) as the loss.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Both are mathematically the same model. The from_logits route lets the loss compute log-softmax with the log-sum-exp trick, which is more numerically stable than computing softmax and then taking its log, especially in low precision (mixed precision is on, p.499). The cost: model.predict() then returns logits, so you must apply softmax yourself if you want probabilities.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the standard pattern for language models and, increasingly, for classifiers in general.

terminology.meaning: Cross-entropy where the target is an integer class index rather than a one-hot vector.

connections: p.501: the loss used in Listing 16.8

paragraphs.excerpt: After training, our model can predict the next token in a sequence about
paragraphs.what_it_says: After training, the model predicts the next token correctly about 36% of the time on the validation set, though such a metric is just a crude heuristic.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Accuracy counts a hit only when the argmax token is exactly the true next token. Language is inherently uncertain: after 'I would like a cup of' both 'tea' and 'coffee' are good continuations, but only one is counted correct. Accuracy also ignores how much probability the model gave to the right answer, which the loss (and perplexity, its exponential) captures. Still, 36% top-1 over a 32,000-token vocabulary is far above chance (1/32,000).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a rough benchmark; p.517 compares a fine-tuned Gemma's 55% against mini-GPT (cited there as 35%) to show the effect of scale.

terminology.meaning: Fraction of positions where the model's most likely token equals the actual next token.

paragraphs.excerpt: Note that our model is undertrained. Our validation loss will continue to tick down
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model is undertrained: validation loss keeps decreasing every epoch, unsurprising since it used 100x fewer training steps than GPT-1. Training longer would help but needs time and money for compute. The authors then move on to playing with the model.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A validation loss that is still falling at the end of training means the model has not yet reached the point where extra training stops helping (let alone the overfitting point). Since each token was seen only once (p.501), there is little risk of overfitting; the limit is the compute budget.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains why the generated text in the next pages is mediocre and foreshadows the switch to a properly trained pretrained model (p.508).

terminology.meaning: A model whose loss would still improve substantially with more training.

connections: p.501: 100x fewer training steps than GPT-1
p.530: even GPT-3 is now known to have been undertrained

paragraphs.excerpt: To sample some output from our model, we can follow the approach we used
paragraphs.what_it_says: Generation follows the chapter 15 approach: feed a prompt, get a distribution over the vocabulary for the next token at each position, pick the most likely next token at the last position, append it and repeat, generating one token at a time.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is autoregressive decoding: each new token is conditioned on everything generated so far. Because training used a causal mask, the outputs at the last position depend on the whole prefix and predict the token that follows it. Always taking the most likely token is greedy decoding (named on p.505).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It is the basic inference loop of every GPT-style model, including ChatGPT-style systems; later pages change only how the next token is chosen and how fast each step runs.

terminology.meaning: Producing a sequence one element at a time, feeding each output back as input.
The initial fixed tokens given to the model to continue.

connections: p.505: picking the most likely token is called greedy search

concepts.name: Logits
concepts.definition: Unnormalized log probabilities output by a model before softmax.
concepts.intuition: Raw scores: higher means more likely, but they do not sum to anything in particular.
concepts.technical: z_i = log p_i + C. softmax(z) = exp(z) / sum(exp(z)) recovers p. Adding a constant to all logits does not change the probabilities.
concepts.significance: Losses with from_logits=True and samplers operate directly on logits, which is numerically stable and makes temperature scaling trivial.
concepts.misconception: Logits are not probabilities and can be negative or larger than 1.

concepts.name: Softmax
concepts.definition: Function mapping a score vector to a probability distribution by exponentiating and normalizing.
concepts.intuition: Make everything positive, then divide by the total.
concepts.technical: softmax(z)_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j); monotonic, so it preserves the ranking of the scores.
concepts.significance: Can sit at the end of the model or inside the loss; mini-GPT puts it inside the loss.
concepts.misconception: You do not need softmax to pick the most likely token: argmax of logits is the same.

concepts.name: Greedy decoding
concepts.definition: Generating text by always appending the single most likely next token.
concepts.intuition: Always take the locally best step without looking ahead.
concepts.technical: next = argmax_i z_i at the last position; deterministic: the same prompt always gives the same output.
concepts.significance: Simple baseline; prone to repetition loops, as p.503 and p.504 show.
concepts.misconception: The most likely token at each step does not give the most likely whole sequence.

concepts.name: Autoregressive language model
concepts.definition: A model that outputs a distribution over the next token given the previous ones and can generate text by feeding its outputs back in.
concepts.technical: Trained with a causal mask so position t only sees tokens up to t; at inference the last position's output is the next-token distribution.
concepts.significance: Mini-GPT, GPT-1 and Gemma are all of this type.
concepts.example: Prompt 'A piece of advice' -> model predicts ',' -> appended -> repeat.
concepts.misconception: The model does not plan a whole sentence ahead; it only ever produces one next-token distribution at a time.

math.title: From logits to probabilities (softmax)
math.source_text: If you exponentiate each output value and normalize all values to sum to 1 (this is all the softmax function does), you will get a probability value.

variables.meaning: Logit (model output) for vocabulary token i
Probability of token i being the next token

math.operations: Exponentiate each logit, divide by the sum of all exponentials. The second form shows that a logit is a log probability plus a shared constant (the log normalizer), hence 'unnormalized log probability'.
math.purpose: Formalizes the sidebar's definition of a logit.
math.interpretation: Differences between logits are what matter: z_i - z_j = log(p_i / p_j).
math.intuition: Logits are scores on a log scale; softmax converts them to shares of 100%.

math.title: Greedy choice in Listing 16.9

variables.meaning: Logits at the last position of the current sequence (prediction[0, -1])
The token appended to the sequence

math.purpose: Shows why no softmax is needed in the generation loop.
math.interpretation: Softmax is strictly increasing in each logit, so it never changes which entry is largest.
math.intuition: The tallest bar stays the tallest whether you measure in logits or probabilities.

code.title: A simple generation function for the mini-GPT model
code.what_it_does: Greedy autoregressive generation: extends a text prompt to max_length tokens by repeatedly running mini-GPT on the whole current sequence and appending the highest-scoring next token.

line_explanations.explanation: max_length is the total length of the output in tokens, prompt included (64 by default, well under the 256-token context the model was trained with).
Tokenize the prompt with the tokenizer from p.495-496, convert to NumPy and then to a Python list (easy to append to); remember its length.
Generate exactly max_length - prompt_length new tokens.

Wrap the list in another list to make a batch of one, shape (1, current_length), and call the model directly. Output: logits of shape (1, current_length, 32000). This direct call is uncompiled and the input shape grows every iteration, the two reasons p.503 gives for its slowness.
Keep only the logits at the last position of the single sequence: a vector of 32,000 scores for the next token.
Greedy choice: argmax of the logits (no softmax needed), .item() turns the NumPy integer into a Python int, appended to the sequence.
Convert the full id list (prompt plus generated tokens) back to text.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a prompt string, e.g. 'A piece of advice' (p.503). Output: a string of max_length tokens beginning with the prompt.
code.algorithm: for t in prompt_length .. max_length-1: logits = model(tokens); tokens.append(argmax(logits[last])). Each step reprocesses the whole prefix, so total work grows roughly quadratically with output length.
code.theory_link: Autoregressive decoding of a causal language model; greedy search (p.505).

parameters.name: max_length
parameters.role: Total sequence length in tokens; must not exceed the positional-embedding length (256).

pitfalls: Calling the model directly runs uncompiled; generation takes minutes (p.503).
The input shape changes every step, which would force recompilation if you naively switched to predict() (p.503).
Greedy decoding is deterministic and tends to loop on high-probability phrases (p.503-504).
Prompts longer than max_length make range() empty, so the function returns the prompt unchanged.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: inspect the top-5 candidates at one step
import numpy as np
tokens = list(ops.convert_to_numpy(tokenizer("A piece of advice")))
logits = ops.convert_to_numpy(mini_gpt(np.array([tokens]))[0, -1])
probs = np.exp(logits - logits.max()); probs /= probs.sum()
for i in np.argsort(-probs)[:5]:
    print(repr(tokenizer.detokenize([int(i)])), round(float(probs[i]), 3))

deeper.title: Why put the softmax in the loss?
deeper.body: Cross-entropy needs $\log p_y$. Computing $p = \operatorname{softmax}(z)$ first and then $\log p_y$ can fail: if $p_y$ underflows to 0 (easy with 32,000 classes and, under mixed precision, float16 activations), the log is $-\infty$. With logits, the loss computes $\log p_y = z_y - \log\sum_j e^{z_j}$ using the log-sum-exp trick (subtract $\max_j z_j$ before exponentiating), which never overflows or underflows badly. This is why `from_logits=True` is the standard choice for language models. (Explanation beyond the book.)

deeper.title: Why 36% is both impressive and limited
deeper.body: Random guessing over 32,000 tokens would be right $1/32000 \approx 0.003\%$ of the time, so 36% is about 11,500x better than chance. But many next tokens are genuinely unpredictable (names, numbers, content words), so even a perfect model of English would be far from 100%. That is why the authors call accuracy 'a crude heuristic'; the validation loss (average negative log-probability of the true token) is a more informative measure, and its continued decrease is what reveals that the model is undertrained.

deeper.title: Analogy: autocomplete on repeat
deeper.body: Type a phrase on your phone, then keep tapping the middle (most likely) suggestion. You get fluent-looking but repetitive text, exactly the behaviour mini-GPT shows on p.503 with greedy decoding.

misconceptions.correction: A logit is an unnormalized log probability; only after softmax does it become a probability.

misconceptions.claim: You must apply softmax before picking the most likely token.
misconceptions.correction: Softmax preserves order, so np.argmax on the logits gives the same token; Listing 16.9 never calls softmax.

misconceptions.claim: 36% accuracy means the model is bad at language.
misconceptions.correction: It is far above chance for a 32,000-token vocabulary; accuracy is a crude measure because many next tokens are legitimately ambiguous. The model is, however, undertrained.
It only tells the loss function what kind of values it receives.

takeaways: A logit is an unnormalized log probability; softmax (exponentiate, normalize) turns logits into probabilities.
Keras lets you put softmax in the model or in the loss; with logits outputs use SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True).
Mini-GPT reaches about 36% next-token validation accuracy, a crude measure, and is still undertrained.
Generative decoding repeatedly feeds the sequence back and appends the predicted token at the last position.
Listing 16.9 uses greedy selection (argmax of logits) and calls the model directly on a growing sequence.

questions.question: Which statement about logits is correct?
options: They sum to 1 across the vocabulary
Applying softmax to them yields probabilities, and their argmax equals the argmax of those probabilities
They are the log of the probabilities, with no extra constant
questions.answer: Applying softmax to them yields probabilities, and their argmax equals the argmax of those probabilities
questions.explanation: Logits are unnormalized log probabilities: unbounded, not summing to 1, and equal to log probabilities only up to an additive constant (hence 'unnormalized'). Softmax is monotonic, so it preserves the argmax.

questions.question: A model outputs logits [3, 1, 1] for three tokens. Compute the softmax probabilities. What happens if you add 10 to every logit?
questions.answer: e^3 = 20.09, e^1 = 2.718 twice; sum 25.52; probabilities about [0.787, 0.107, 0.107]. Adding 10 to all logits leaves them unchanged.
questions.explanation: The common factor e^10 cancels between numerator and denominator, which is why logits are only defined up to an additive constant.

questions.question: What are the two options Keras gives for where to apply the softmax in a classifier, and what must you do for the second?
questions.answer: Use softmax as the model's last activation (output probabilities), or omit it and move it into the loss (output logits) by passing SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True).
questions.explanation: This is the content of the sidebar's last paragraph.

questions.question: Why do the authors conclude the model is undertrained, and why is that unsurprising?
questions.answer: Validation loss is still decreasing after every epoch; the run used 100x fewer training steps than GPT-1.
questions.explanation: A still-falling validation loss means more training would keep helping. With one pass over ~1 billion tokens and a compute budget far below GPT-1's, there was no chance to converge.

questions.question: In Listing 16.9, what does prediction[0, -1] select?
options: The logits for the first token of the prompt
The logits at the last position of the only sequence in the batch, i.e. the next-token scores
The last vocabulary entry for every position
The probability of the end-of-text token
questions.answer: The logits at the last position of the only sequence in the batch, i.e. the next-token scores
questions.explanation: The model output has shape (1, n, 32000); index 0 picks the single sequence and -1 the last position, leaving 32,000 next-token logits. It is not the first token, not a single vocabulary column, and not a probability.

questions.question: Listing 16.9 calls the model on the entire sequence at every step but uses only the last position's output. Name one inefficiency this causes and where the book addresses it.
questions.answer: It recomputes all previous positions every step (and runs uncompiled with a changing shape). p.503 fixes compilation with predict() and padding; p.504 describes key/value caching to avoid recomputing past positions.
questions.explanation: Work grows with sequence length at each step; caching keys and values makes each step process only one new token.

questions.question: Could you rewrite Listing 16.9 from memory and explain why no softmax appears in it?
questions.answer: Yes if you can reproduce tokenize -> loop(model, last position, argmax, append) -> detokenize and justify that argmax is unchanged by softmax.
questions.explanation: These are the essential ideas of this page: logits and greedy autoregressive decoding.
